title: Boss: the first week on the job
summary: Read a messy working tree, split it into clean commits, and build the tools that model it.

steps.title: The scene
body: It is your first week. You cloned the team's repo, fixed a bug, started a feature, and ran a build. Now `git status -s` is a wall of letters and your lead wants **two clean commits**: the bug fix alone, then the feature.
Everything in this module comes together: the three areas, status codes, diffs, ignore rules and messages.

steps.prompt: Your fix is in `Cart.cs`; the feature touched `Cart.cs` too (a different hunk) and added `Coupon.cs`. `.gitignore` has `bin/`. What does `git status -s` print before you stage anything?
code: # on disk now: Cart.cs (2 changed hunks), Coupon.cs (new), bin/Shop.dll
steps.explain: `Cart.cs` is modified but unstaged. `Coupon.cs` is new. `bin/` is ignored, so the build output is not listed.

steps.prompt: Arrange the commands to produce the two commits: the fix first, then the feature.
lines: git commit -m "Fix rounding in cart total"
steps.explain: `git add -p` lets you stage only the fix hunk. Check it with `git diff --staged`, commit, then stage the rest (the feature hunk and the new file) for the second commit.

steps.title: Stop tracking the local settings
prompt: Last month someone committed `appsettings.Local.json`, which holds a local database password. Adding it to `.gitignore` now does nothing, because Git keeps tracking files it already has.
1. Stop tracking `appsettings.Local.json`, but **keep the file on disk** (the app still reads it).
3. Commit just that (`.gitignore` and the removal), leaving the Cart and Coupon work uncommitted for the next step.

checks.name: the file is no longer tracked
checks.cmd: cd ~/shop && ! git ls-files --error-unmatch appsettings.Local.json 2>/dev/null && ! git cat-file -e HEAD:appsettings.Local.json 2>/dev/null
checks.fail: `appsettings.Local.json` is still tracked or still in the last commit. `git rm --cached` removes it from the index only.

checks.name: the file is still on disk
checks.fail: The file itself is gone. Plain `git rm` deletes it from disk too; press Reset scenario and use `--cached`.

checks.name: it is ignored now
checks.cmd: cd ~/shop && git check-ignore -q appsettings.Local.json && git diff --quiet HEAD -- .gitignore

checks.name: the Cart and Coupon work is still uncommitted
checks.cmd: cd ~/shop && git show HEAD:src/Cart.cs | grep -q 'return sum;' && ! git cat-file -e HEAD:src/Coupon.cs 2>/dev/null && grep -q AwayFromZero src/Cart.cs
checks.fail: This commit should hold the settings change only. The Cart.cs and Coupon.cs edits belong to the next step.

hints: `git rm --cached <file>` untracks a file and leaves it on disk.
Commit with `git commit -m "Stop tracking local settings"`. Do not use `git commit -a`: it would take Cart.cs too.
steps.explain: The password is still in last month's commit, so anyone with the repo can read it: change the password too. `git rm --cached` plus `.gitignore` only stops future commits from carrying the file.

steps.title: Two clean commits with add -p
prompt: `src/Cart.cs` holds two changes: the **bug fix** (rounding in `Total`, the first hunk) and part of the **feature** (the coupon discount, the second hunk). `src/Coupon.cs` is the rest of the feature. `src/bin/` is build output.
Make two commits, in this order:
1. `Fix rounding in cart total`: only the first hunk of `src/Cart.cs`.
2. `Add percentage coupons`: the second hunk and `src/Coupon.cs`.
`git add -p src/Cart.cs` asks about each hunk: answer `y` (stage it) or `n` (skip it), then check with `git diff --staged` before you commit.

checks.name: the fix commit has the rounding change only
checks.cmd: cd ~/shop && test "$(git log -1 --format=%s HEAD~1)" = 'Fix rounding in cart total' && git show HEAD~1:src/Cart.cs | grep -q AwayFromZero && git show HEAD~1:src/Cart.cs | grep -q 'return 0m;' && ! git cat-file -e HEAD~1:src/Coupon.cs 2>/dev/null
checks.fail: The commit before the newest should be `Fix rounding in cart total` and hold only the rounding hunk (no coupon code, no Coupon.cs).

checks.name: the feature commit has the rest
checks.cmd: cd ~/shop && test "$(git log -1 --format=%s)" = 'Add percentage coupons' && git show HEAD:src/Cart.cs | grep -q coupon.Percent && git cat-file -e HEAD:src/Coupon.cs
checks.fail: The newest commit should be `Add percentage coupons` with the discount hunk and `src/Coupon.cs`.

checks.name: build output is not committed and the tree is clean
checks.cmd: cd ~/shop && ! git ls-files | grep -q '^src/bin/' && test -z "$(git status --porcelain)"
checks.fail: `src/bin/` must stay out of history (it is ignored), and nothing else should be left over.

hints: `git add -p src/Cart.cs` shows the first hunk (the `Math.Round` line). Answer `y`, then `n` for the second.
`git diff --staged` should show only the rounding change. Then `git commit -m "Fix rounding in cart total"`.
For the second commit: `git add src/Cart.cs src/Coupon.cs` and `git commit -m "Add percentage coupons"`.
solution: git commit -m "Fix rounding in cart total"
steps.explain: Small, single-purpose commits are easy to review, revert and cherry-pick: the fix can go to a release branch without the feature. `git add -p` also has `s` (split a hunk further) and `e` (edit it). `git restore -p` and `git stash -p` work the same way. (The answer pipes `y` and `n` into `git add -p`; typing them at the prompt is the same.)

steps.title: A message the reviewer can use
prompt: In `~/shop`, a change to `src/Payments.cs` is staged: it retries the payment gateway twice before failing.
Commit it with a message that passes the team's rules (the check runs them on your commit):
- a subject of at most 50 characters, in the imperative (`Retry ...`, not `Retried ...`), starting with a capital, no period at the end;
- a body that says **why** (the gateway times out under load), lines of at most 72 characters.
Two `-m` options make two paragraphs: `git commit -m "Subject" -m "Body ..."`.

checks.name: the newest commit message follows the rules
checks.fail: The message breaks a rule (listed below). Fix it with `git commit --amend -m "Subject" -m "Body"`; amending an unpushed commit is safe.

checks.name: the change is committed
checks.cmd: cd ~/shop && git diff --cached --quiet && git show HEAD:src/Payments.cs | grep -q Retry.Twice
checks.fail: The staged change should be in the newest commit.

hints: Subject: what the commit does, as an order: `Retry payment gateway calls twice`.
Body: the reason and the effect, for example `The gateway times out under load. Retrying twice with a 200 ms backoff saves the order instead of failing it.`
`git commit -m "Retry payment gateway calls twice" -m "The gateway times out under load. ..."`. Wrong already? `git commit --amend -m ... -m ...`.
solution: git commit -m "Retry payment gateway calls twice" -m "The gateway times out under load, which failed orders that would" -m "succeed a moment later. Retry twice with a 200 ms backoff first."
steps.explain: The subject is what `git log --oneline`, GitHub and `git shortlog` show; the body is what someone reads with `git blame` a year from now, asking "why is this here?". Keep the 50/72 shape and say why, not how: the diff already shows how. The gitkit linter you wrote in lesson 4 checks the same rules as a `commit-msg` hook.
